text: Benjamin "Bibi" Netanyahu, born on 21 October 1949 in Tel Aviv, is an Israeli politician and diplomat who has served as Prime Minister of Israel since 2022. He previously held office from 1996 to 1999 and from 2009 to 2021, making him Israel's longest-serving prime minister. Born in Tel Aviv, Netanyahu was raised in West Jerusalem and the United States. He returned to Israel in 1967 to join the Israel Defense Forces and served in the Sayeret Matkal special forces, participating in numerous cross-border raids during the 1967–70 War of Attrition, including the March 1968 Battle of Karameh, and was wounded in combat on multiple occasions. He was involved in the 1968 Israeli raid on Lebanon and the rescue of the hijacked Sabena Flight 571 in May 1972, during which he was shot in the shoulder. He was discharged from active service in 1972 but remained in the Sayeret Matkal reserves. After returning to the United States in late 1972, he studied architecture at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), completing his bachelor's degree in architecture in February 1975 and earning a master's degree from the MIT Sloan School of Management in 1976, while concurrently pursuing a doctorate in political science. He changed his name to Benjamin "Ben" Nitai at MIT to make it easier for Americans to pronounce, a move later used by political rivals to accuse him of lacking Israeli national identity. He worked as an economic consultant for the Boston Consulting Group in Boston, Massachusetts, between 1976 and 1978, where he was a colleague of Mitt Romney. In 1978, he returned to Israel and founded the Yonatan Netanyahu Anti-Terror Institute. Between 1980 and 1982, he served as director of marketing for Rim Industries in Jerusalem. From 1982 to 1984, he served as Deputy Chief of Mission at the Israeli Embassy in Washington, D.C., and during the 1982 Lebanon War, he was called up for reserve duty in Sayeret Matkal, requesting to be released to serve as a spokesperson for Israel amid international criticism. Between 1984 and 1988, he served as Israel's ambassador to the United Nations. Netanyahu rose to prominence after being elected chair of Likud in 1993, becoming leader of the opposition. In the 1996 general election, he became the first Israeli prime minister elected directly by popular vote, defeating the pre-election favorite Shimon Peres, whose government was weakened by a wave of suicide bombings, including the Dizengoff Center and Jaffa Road bus bombings. Netanyahu won the election with the campaign slogan "Netanyahu – making a safe peace" and formed a coalition with the ultra-Orthodox parties Shas and UTJ. He met Palestinian President Yasser Arafat on 4 September 1996 and later signed the Hebron Protocol on 14 January 1997. In 1996, Netanyahu and Jerusalem's mayor Ehud Olmert opened an exit in the Arab Quarter for the Western Wall Tunnel, which sparked three days of rioting. The peace process stalled, leading to the Wye River Memorandum in 1998, which was signed by Netanyahu and Arafat and approved by the Knesset by 75–19. Netanyahu emphasized a policy of "three no(s)": no withdrawal from the Golan Heights, no discussion of Jerusalem, and no negotiations under any preconditions. In 1997, Hamas launched a bombing campaign, including the 30 July Mahane Yehuda market and 4 September Ben Yehuda street bombings, killing 21 Israelis. In response, Netanyahu authorized a Mossad operation to assassinate Hamas leader Khaled Meshal in Jordan, which was exposed, leading to arrests and a crisis with King Hussein, who demanded the release of Palestinian prisoners and threatened to annul the Israeli-Jordanian peace treaty. Netanyahu relented under pressure from U.S. President Bill Clinton and ordered the release of 61 Jordanian and Palestinian prisoners, including Sheikh Ahmed Yassin. On the same day as the Ben Yehuda bombings, Hezbollah executed the Ansariya ambush on the IDF's naval special forces Shayetet 13. Netanyahu returned to lead Likud in 2005, leading the opposition between 2006 and 2009. After the 2009 legislative election, he formed a coalition and became prime minister again. From 2016, he made his closeness to Donald Trump central to his appeal. During Trump's first presidency, the U.S. recognized Jerusalem as the capital of Israel, affirmed Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights, and brokered the Abraham Accords between Israel and the Arab world. Netanyahu faced criticism for expanding Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, deemed illegal under international law. In 2019, he was indicted on charges of breach of trust, bribery, and fraud, and relinquished all ministerial posts except prime minister. The 2018–2022 Israeli political crisis resulted in a rotation agreement between Netanyahu and Benny Gantz, which collapsed in 2020, leading to a 2021 election. In June 2021, Netanyahu was removed from the premiership before returning after the 2022 election. His premierships have been criticized for perceived democratic backsliding and an alleged shift towards authoritarianism. His coalition pursued judicial reform, which triggered large-scale protests in early 2023. The October 7 attacks by Hamas-led Palestinian groups in 2023 triggered the Gaza war, with Netanyahu facing nationwide protests over the security lapse and failure to secure the return of Israeli hostages. In October 2024, he survived an assassination attempt and ordered an invasion of Lebanon to destroy Hezbollah's military capabilities. After the fall of the Assad regime in December 2024, Netanyahu directed an invasion of Syria. He also presided over the 2025 Israeli strikes on Iran, which escalated into the Iran–Israel war. Netanyahu's government has been accused of orchestrating the genocide in Gaza, culminating in the South Africa v. Israel case before the International Court of Justice in December 2023. The International Criminal Court (ICC) issued an arrest warrant in November 2024 for Netanyahu for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity as part of the ICC investigation in Palestine. His mother, Tzila Segal, was born in Petah Tikva in the Mutasarrifate of Jerusalem, with her family having migrated from Minneapolis in 1911, originally from Lithuania in the 1870s, and studied law at Gray's Inn, London. His father, Benzion Netanyahu (né Mileikowsky), was a historian specializing in the Jewish Golden Age of Spain, and his paternal grandfather, Nathan Mileikowsky, was a rabbi and Zionist writer. When Benzion immigrated to Mandatory Palestine, he adopted the Hebrew surname "Netanyahu," meaning "God has given." Netanyahu's family is predominantly Ashkenazi, though he claims some Sephardic ancestry and descent from the Vilna Gaon. He is the second of three children and was initially raised in Jerusalem, attending Henrietta Szold Elementary School, where his 6th-grade teacher Ruth Rubenstein noted he was courteous, polite, responsible, punctual, friendly, disciplined, cheerful, brave, active, and obedient. Between 1956 and 1958, and from 1963 to 1967, his family lived in Cheltenham Township, Pennsylvania, while his father taught at Dropsie College. Netanyahu graduated from Cheltenham High School and was active in the debate club, chess club, and soccer. He and his brother Yonatan grew dissatisfied with the superficial lifestyle and liberal sensibilities of the Reform synagogue, Temple Judea of Philadelphia. After graduating from high school in 1967, Netanyahu returned to Israel to enlist in the Israel Defense Forces, trained as a combat soldier, and served for five years in Sayeret Matkal. He was wounded in combat multiple times and was involved in the 1968 Israeli raid on Lebanon and the rescue of Sabena Flight 571. He was discharged in 1972 but remained in the reserves. After returning to the United States in late 1972, he studied architecture at MIT, completed his bachelor's degree in two and a half years despite a break for the Yom Kippur War, and earned a master's degree in 1976. He studied political science toward a doctorate, which was interrupted by the death of his brother Yonatan during the Entebbe raid. Professor Leon B. Groisser at MIT described him as "very bright, organized, strong, powerful, knowing what he wanted and how to get it done." Netanyahu changed his name to Benjamin "Ben" Nitai at MIT to make it easier for Americans to pronounce, a move criticized by political rivals as indicating a lack of Israeli loyalty. He worked at the Boston Consulting Group from 1976 to 1978, where he was a colleague of Mitt Romney. In 1978, he appeared on Boston local television under the name "Ben Nitay," arguing that the core of the conflict was the Arab refusal to accept Israel and that Palestinians could have established a Palestinian state. In 1978, he returned to Israel and ran the Jonathan Netanyahu Anti-Terror Institute from 1978 to 1980. From 1980 to 1982, he was director of marketing for Rim Industries in Jerusalem. He served as Deputy Chief of Mission at the Israeli Embassy in Washington, D.C., from 1982 to 1984. During the 1982 Lebanon War, he was called up for reserve duty and requested to be released to serve as a spokesperson. He established an efficient public relations system at the Israeli embassy. He was influenced by Rabbi Menachem M. Schneerson, whom he called "the most influential man of our time," and became friends with Fred Trump, father of future U.S. President Donald Trump. Prior to the 1988 Israeli legislative election, he joined the Likud party, was placed fifth on the party list, and was elected to the 12th Knesset. He served as deputy to foreign ministers Moshe Arens and David Levy, with whom he had a rivalry. During the Gulf War in early 1991, Netanyahu emerged as the principal spokesman for Israel in media interviews. He was a member of the Israeli delegation at the Madrid Conference of 1991 and later appointed Deputy Minister in the Prime Minister's Office. After the Likud's defeat in the 1992 elections, Netanyahu won the 1993 party leadership election, defeating Benny Begin and David Levy. Following the assassination of Yitzhak Rabin, Shimon Peres called early elections to advance the peace process. Netanyahu was the Likud's candidate in the 1996 election, which was the first direct election for prime minister, and won, becoming the youngest person to hold the office and the first Israeli prime minister born in the State of Israel. Peres's Labor Party received more seats, but Netanyahu formed a coalition with Shas and UTJ. The months leading up to the 1996 election were marked by Hamas attacks, including the assassination of Yahya Ayyash on 5 January 1996, which led to a bombing campaign by Hamas, including the Dizengoff Center and Jaffa Road bus bombings, allegedly planned and financed with Syrian and Iranian support. According to a report, Syrian Defense Minister Mustafa Tlass instructed Ghazi Kanaan to establish links between Hezbollah and Hamas fighters, who were trained in Lebanon and Iran. Hamas operative Hassan Salameh, trained in Iran, planned several attacks. Ronen Bergman attributes the defeat of Peres and the Likud's victory to the bombing campaign and the Israeli intelligence services' failure to prevent it, noting that attacks ceased for almost a year after Netanyahu halted the peace process. Netanyahu first met Arafat on 4 September 1996, and their talks culminated in the Hebron Protocol on 14 January 1997. In 1996, Netanyahu and Olmert opened an exit in the Arab Quarter for the Western Wall Tunnel, which triggered three days of rioting. The Wye River Memorandum in 1998 detailed steps to implement the 1995 Interim Agreement and was approved by the Knesset 75–19. Netanyahu emphasized the "three no(s)" policy. In 1997, Ali Fallahian, the Iranian Intelligence Minister, authorized a Hamas bombing campaign, with Hamas leader Khaled Meshal sending suicide bombers to attack Jerusalem, killing 21 Israelis. Netanyahu authorized a Mossad operation to assassinate Meshal in Jordan, which was exposed, leading to arrests and a crisis with King Hussein, who demanded the release of Palestinian prisoners and threatened to annul the peace treaty. Netanyahu relented under U.S. pressure and released 61 prisoners, including Sheikh Ahmed Yassin. The incident damaged Israeli-Jordanian relations. The antidote secured the release of two agents, but at least six others were holed up in the Israeli embassy, and King Hussein demanded the release of Ahmed Yassin and many other prisoners. On the same day as the Ben Yehuda bombings, Hezbollah executed the Ansariya ambush on Shayetet 13.

Five Canadian tourists entered Jordan on 27 September and injected poison into Mashal's ears in a street in Amman. The plot was exposed, and two agents were arrested by Jordanian police, while three others hid in the Israeli embassy, which was then surrounded by troops. An angry King Hussein demanded Israel provide the antidote and threatened to annul the peace treaty. Netanyahu relented under pressure from US President Bill Clinton and ordered the release of 61 Jordanian and Palestinian prisoners, including Sheikh Ahmad Yassin. The incident severely damaged nascent Israeli-Jordanian relations. Mashal's antidote only secured the release of the two Mossad Kidon agents involved in the assassination attempt; at least six other Mossad agents were holed up in the Israeli embassy. King Hussein would only release them if Israel released Ahmed Yassin and a large number of other Palestinian prisoners, as the demands needed to be "enough to enable the king to be able to publicly defend the release of the hit team." On the same day Hamas bombed Ben Yehuda Street, Hezbollah executed the Ansariya ambush on the IDF's naval special forces Shayetet 13, killing 12 Israeli commandos. On 25 May 1998, the remains and body parts of at least three soldiers who died in the Ansariya ambush were exchanged for 65 Lebanese prisoners and the bodies of 40 Hizbullah fighters and Lebanese soldiers captured by Israel. Netanyahu called it "one of the worst tragedies that has ever occurred to us." Netanyahu began a process of economic liberalization, selling government shares in banks and state-run companies, easing foreign exchange controls, enabling Israelis to take unrestricted amounts of money out of the country, open foreign bank accounts, hold foreign currency, and invest freely. Netanyahu was opposed by the left and lost support from the right due to concessions to Palestinians in Hebron and elsewhere, and his negotiations with Arafat. He lost public favor after scandals involving his marriage and corruption charges. In 1997, police recommended Netanyahu be indicted on corruption charges for influence-peddling; he was accused of appointing an attorney general to reduce charges, but prosecutors ruled there was insufficient evidence for trial. In 1999, Netanyahu faced another scandal when the Israel Police recommended he be tried for corruption over $100,000 in free services from a government contractor; Israel's attorney general did not prosecute, citing evidence difficulties. Israeli failures against Hamas and Hezbollah under Netanyahu's first premiership, and the resulting release of imprisoned Palestinian and Lebanese leaders, undermined his "tough stance" rhetoric and contributed to his defeat in the 1999 Israeli general election. After losing to Ehud Barak in the 1999 prime ministerial election, Netanyahu temporarily retired from politics. He served as a senior consultant with BATM Advanced Communications for two years. With the fall of the Barak government in late 2000, Netanyahu expressed a desire to return to politics. By law, Barak's resignation was supposed to lead to prime ministerial elections only; Netanyahu insisted on general elections, claiming otherwise a stable government would be impossible. He decided not to run for prime minister, facilitating Ariel Sharon's rise to power. In 2002, after the Labor Party left the coalition and vacated the foreign minister position, Prime Minister Ariel Sharon appointed Netanyahu as foreign minister. Netanyahu challenged Sharon for leadership of the Likud party in the 2002 leadership election but failed to oust him. On 9 September 2002, a scheduled speech by Netanyahu at Concordia University in Montreal, Quebec, Canada was canceled after hundreds of pro-Palestinian protesters overwhelmed security and smashed through a window. Netanyahu was not present at the protest, having remained at his hotel. He later accused the activists of supporting terrorism and "mad zealotry." Weeks later in October, around 200 protesters met Netanyahu outside his Heinz Hall appearance in Pittsburgh. Pittsburgh Police, Israeli security, and a Pittsburgh SWAT unit allowed his speeches to continue downtown at the hall and the Duquesne Club as well as at Robert Morris University. On 12 September 2002, Netanyahu lobbied for the invasion of Iraq, testifying under oath as a private citizen before the U.S. House of Representatives Government Reform Committee regarding the alleged nuclear threat posed by the Iraqi regime: "There is no question whatsoever that Saddam is seeking and is working and is advancing towards the development of nuclear weapons…" He also testified, "If you take out Saddam, Saddam's regime, I guarantee you that it will have enormous positive reverberations on the region." After the 2003 Israeli legislative election, Sharon offered the Foreign Ministry to Silvan Shalom and offered Netanyahu the Finance Ministry. Some pundits speculated Sharon made the move because he viewed Netanyahu as a political threat due to his effectiveness as foreign minister, and that placing him in Finance during economic uncertainty would diminish his popularity. Netanyahu accepted the appointment. Sharon and Netanyahu agreed that Netanyahu would have complete freedom as finance minister and have Sharon restore all his reforms in exchange for Netanyahu's silence on Sharon's military and foreign affairs. As finance minister, Netanyahu implemented an economic plan to restore Israel's economy from its low point during the Second Intifada. He claimed a bloated public sector and excessive regulations were responsible for stifling growth. His plan included moving toward liberalized markets, ending welfare dependency by requiring job applications or training, reducing the public sector, freezing government spending for three years, capping the budget deficit at 1%, streamlining taxes with the top individual rate reduced from 64% to 44% and the corporate rate from 36% to 18%, privatizing state assets worth billions including banks, oil refineries, El Al, and Zim Integrated Shipping Services, raising retirement ages for both men and women, liberalizing currency exchange laws, forcing commercial banks to spin off long-term savings, and attacking monopolies and cartels to increase competition. As the economy boomed and unemployment fell significantly, Netanyahu was widely credited with performing an "economic miracle." Opponents in the Labor party and some within Likud viewed his policies as "Thatcherite" attacks on the Israeli social safety net. Ultimately, unemployment declined, economic growth soared, the debt-to-GDP ratio dropped to one of the lowest in the world, and foreign investment reached record highs. Netanyahu threatened to resign in 2004 unless the Gaza pullout plan was put to a referendum. He later modified the ultimatum and voted for the program in the Knesset, indicating immediately thereafter that he would resign unless a referendum was held within 14 days. He submitted his resignation letter on 7 August 2005, shortly before the Israeli cabinet voted 17 to 5 to approve the initial phase of withdrawal from Gaza. Following Sharon's exit from the Likud, Netanyahu was one of several candidates vying for the party leadership. His most recent attempt prior to this was in September 2005 when he tried to hold early primaries for the head of the Likud party while the party held the office of prime minister—effectively pushing Ariel Sharon out of office. The party rejected this initiative. Netanyahu retook the leadership on 20 December 2005 with 47% of the primary vote, to 32% for Silvan Shalom and 15% for Moshe Feiglin. In the March 2006 Knesset elections, Likud took third place behind Kadima and Labor, and Netanyahu served as Leader of the Opposition. On 14 August 2007, Netanyahu was reelected as chairman of the Likud and its candidate for prime minister with 73% of the vote, against far-right candidate Moshe Feiglin and World Likud chairman Danny Danon. He opposed the 2008 Israel–Hamas ceasefire, like others in the Knesset opposition, stating: "This is not a relaxation, it's an Israeli agreement to the rearming of Hamas... What are we getting for this?" Following Tzipi Livni's election to head Kadima and Olmert's resignation as prime minister, Netanyahu declined to join the coalition Livni was trying to form and supported new elections held in February 2009. Netanyahu was the Likud's candidate for prime minister in the 2009 Israeli legislative election on 10 February 2009, as Livni, the previous acting prime minister, had been unable to form a viable coalition. Opinion polls showed Likud in the lead, but with as many as a third of Israeli voters undecided. In the election, Likud won the second highest number of seats, Livni's party having outnumbered the Likud by one seat. A possible explanation for Likud's relatively poor showing is that some supporters defected to Avigdor Lieberman's Yisrael Beiteinu party. Netanyahu claimed victory on the basis that right-wing parties won a majority of the vote, and on 20 February 2009, Netanyahu was designated by Israeli President Shimon Peres to succeed Ehud Olmert as prime minister and began negotiations to form a coalition government. Despite right-wing parties winning a majority of 65 seats in the Knesset, Netanyahu preferred a broader centrist coalition and turned to his Kadima rivals, chaired by Tzipi Livni, to join his government. This time it was Livni who declined to join, due to differences on how to pursue the peace process. Netanyahu managed to entice the Labor Party, chaired by Ehud Barak, to join his government, giving him a centrist tone. Netanyahu presented his cabinet for a Knesset "Vote of Confidence" on 31 March 2009. The 32nd Government was approved by a majority of 69 lawmakers to 45 (with five abstaining) and the members were sworn in. In 2009, US Secretary of State Hillary Clinton voiced support for establishing a Palestinian state—a solution not endorsed by Netanyahu, with whom she had pledged US cooperation. Netanyahu stated negotiations with the Palestinians would be conditioned on them recognizing Israel as a Jewish state. During Obama's 2009 Cairo speech, Obama stated the US did not accept the legitimacy of continued Israeli settlements. On 14 June, ten days after Obama's speech, Netanyahu gave a speech endorsing a "Demilitarized Palestinian State." He stated he would accept a Palestinian state if Jerusalem remained the united capital of Israel, Palestinians had no army, and gave up their right of return. He argued for a "natural growth" in existing Jewish settlements in the West Bank, with their permanent status up for negotiation. He endorsed a Palestinian state for the first time alongside Israel, stating he would be willing to meet with any "Arab leader" for negotiations without preconditions, mentioning Syria, Saudi Arabia, and Lebanon. The address represented a new position for Netanyahu's government. Right-wing members of Netanyahu's coalition criticized his remarks on a Palestinian state, believing all land should come under Israeli sovereignty. Opposition party Kadima leader Tzipi Livni opined that Netanyahu did not truly believe in the two-state solution and that the speech was a response to international pressure. Netanyahu's speech provoked mixed international reactions. The Palestinian Authority rejected the conditions on a Palestinian state. Palestinian official Saeb Erekat said the speech had "closed the door to permanent status negotiations" due to Netanyahu's declarations on Jerusalem, refugees, and settlements. Hamas called it "racist" and called on Arab nations to "form stronger opposition." The Arab League dismissed the speech, declaring "Arabs would not make concessions regarding issues of Jerusalem and refugees." The EU noted "...this is a step in the right direction. The acceptance of a Palestinian state was present there." Obama's press secretary said the speech was an "important step forward." Obama said "this solution can and must ensure both Israel's security and the Palestinians' legitimate aspirations for a viable state." France praised the speech and called on Israel to cease building settlements in the West Bank. Three months after starting his term, Netanyahu remarked that his cabinet had established a working national unity government and broad consensus for a "two-state solution." A July 2009 survey found most Israelis supported the government, giving Netanyahu an approval rating of 49 percent. Netanyahu lifted checkpoints in the West Bank to allow free movement and flow of imports, resulting in an economic boost. In 2009, Netanyahu welcomed the Arab Peace initiative and lauded a call by Bahrain's Crown Prince to normalize relations with Israel. In August 2009, Netanyahu said: "We want...recognition of Israel as the national state of the Jewish people and...a security settlement." Palestinian Authority chairman Mahmoud Abbas declared he would be willing to meet with Netanyahu at the UN General Assembly, where Netanyahu had accepted Obama's invitation for a "triple summit." Netanyahu was reported to be in a pivotal moment, considering a compromise over permission for continuing already-approved construction in the West Bank, in exchange for a temporary settlement freeze, continuing building in East Jerusalem, and stopping demolition of Arab houses there. In September, it was reported Netanyahu agreed to settlers' political demands to approve more settlement constructions before a temporary settlement freeze agreement took place. White House spokesman Robert Gibbs expressed regret over the move. On 7 September, Netanyahu left his office without reporting his destination. His military secretary reported he had visited a security facility in Israel. On 9 September, Yedioth Ahronoth reported he had made a secret flight to Moscow to try to persuade Russian officials not to sell S-300 anti-aircraft missile systems to Iran. Headlines branded Netanyahu a "liar" and dubbed the affair a "fiasco." The military secretary was reportedly dismissed. The Sunday Times reported the trip was made to share the names of Russian scientists Israel believed were abetting Iran's nuclear weapons program. On 24 September 2009, in an address to the UN General Assembly, Netanyahu said Iran posed a threat to world peace and it was incumbent on the UN to prevent it from obtaining nuclear weapons. Waving blueprints for Auschwitz and invoking the memory of his family members murdered by the Nazis, Netanyahu delivered a riposte to Iranian president Mahmoud Ahmadinejad's questioning of the Holocaust, asking: "Have you no shame?" In response to pressure from the Obama administration urging the resumption of peace talks, on 25 November Netanyahu announced a partial 10-month settlement construction freeze. It had no significant effect on actual settlement construction. U.S. special envoy George J. Mitchell said, "while the United States shares Arab concerns about the limitations of Israel's gesture, it is more than any Israeli government has ever done." Netanyahu called the move "a painful step that will encourage the peace process" and urged the Palestinians to respond. The Palestinians rejected the call, stating the gesture was "insignificant" because thousands of approved settlement buildings in the West Bank would continue to be built and there would be no freeze of settlement activity in East Jerusalem. In March 2010, Israel's government approved construction of an additional 1,600 apartments in a Jewish housing development in northeast Jerusalem called Ramat Shlomo, despite the U.S. position that such acts thwart peace talks. The announcement occurred during a visit by U.S. Vice President Joe Biden and the U.S. publicly condemned the plan. Netanyahu issued a statement that all previous Israeli governments had continuously permitted construction in the neighborhood, and certain neighborhoods had always been included as part of Israel in any final agreement plan proposed by either side. Netanyahu regretted the timing of the announcement but asserted that "our policy on Jerusalem is the same policy followed by all Israeli governments for the 42 years...it has not changed." In September 2010, Netanyahu agreed to enter direct talks, mediated by the Obama administration, with the Palestinians. The aim was a "final status settlement" to the Israeli–Palestinian conflict by forming a two-state solution for the Jewish and Palestinian people. On 27 September, the 10-month settlement freeze ended, and the Israeli government approved new construction in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem. On retirement in 2011, US Defense Secretary Robert Gates said Netanyahu was ungrateful to the US and endangering Israel. The Likud party defended Netanyahu by saying most Israelis supported him and he had broad support in the US. In 2012, Netanyahu officially recognized for the first time the right for Palestinians to have their own state in an official document.

All previous Israeli governments had consistently permitted construction in the neighborhood, and certain neighborhoods had always been included as part of Israel in any final agreement plan proposed by either side. Netanyahu regretted the timing of the announcement but stated that "our policy on Jerusalem is the same policy followed by all Israeli governments for the 42 years...it has not changed." In September 2010, Netanyahu agreed to enter direct talks, mediated by the Obama administration, with the Palestinians, aiming for a "final status settlement" and a two-state solution. On 27 September, the 10-month settlement freeze ended, and the Israeli government approved new construction in the West Bank, including East Jerusalem. Upon retiring in 2011, US Defense Secretary Robert Gates criticized Netanyahu as ungrateful to the US and endangering Israel, though the Likud party defended him by noting broad support among Israelis and in the US. In 2012, Netanyahu officially recognized for the first time the right of Palestinians to have their own state in a letter to Mahmoud Abbas, though he reiterated that it would have to be demilitarized. Netanyahu unsuccessfully called for the early release of Jonathan Pollard, an American serving a life sentence for passing secret US documents to Israel in 1987; he raised the issue at the Wye River Summit in 1998, claiming President Bill Clinton had privately agreed to release Pollard, and visited Pollard in prison in 2002, maintaining contact with his wife and pressing the Obama administration to release him. In 2011, social justice protests in Israel saw hundreds of thousands protest high living costs; Netanyahu appointed the Trajtenberg Committee, which submitted recommendations to lower living costs, though internal coalition differences led to gradual adoption. Netanyahu's cabinet approved a plan to build a fiber-optic cable network to provide cheap, high-speed Internet access to every home. In 2012, Netanyahu planned early elections but oversaw the creation of a government of national unity to prepare for the 2013 elections; in October 2012, he and Foreign Minister Avigdor Lieberman announced a merger between Likud and Yisrael Beiteinu to run together on a single ballot in the 2013 elections. The 2013 election returned Netanyahu's Likud Beiteinu coalition with 11 fewer seats than the combined parties had going into the vote; Israeli President Shimon Peres tasked Netanyahu with forming the Thirty-third government. During his third term, Netanyahu continued economic liberalization; in December 2013, the Knesset approved the Business Concentration Law, which banned multi-tiered corporate holding structures and limited corporations from owning more than two tiers of publicly listed companies or holding both financial and non-financial enterprises, with all conglomerates given four to six years to sell excess holdings. Netanyahu also launched a campaign of port privatization to break what he viewed as a monopoly by the Israel Port Authority, issuing tenders in July 2013 for private ports in Haifa and Ashdod, and pledged to reduce bureaucracy and regulations to ease industry burdens. In April and June 2014, Netanyahu expressed deep concerns over Hamas and the Palestinian Authority forming a unity government, criticizing both the US and European governments for working with the Palestinian coalition; he blamed Hamas for the kidnapping and murder of three Israeli teenagers in June 2014 and launched a massive search and arrest operation in the West Bank, targeting Hamas members and hitting 60 targets in Gaza. Missile and rocket exchanges escalated after the bodies of the teenagers were discovered on 30 June 2014; after several Hamas operatives were killed, Hamas declared it would launch rockets into Israel, prompting Israel to start Operation Protective Edge, formally ending the November 2012 ceasefire. Netanyahu described Hamas as "genocidal terrorists" in a CNN interview and stated that Hamas was working toward a "third intifada" when asked about Gazan casualties. In October 2014, Netanyahu's government approved a privatization plan to reduce corruption and strengthen Israel's capital market, including minority stakes of up to 49% in state-owned companies such as arms manufacturers, energy, postal, water, railway, and ports of Haifa and Ashdod. That month, Netanyahu called criticism of settlements "against the American values," drawing rebuke from White House Press Secretary Josh Earnest, who noted that American values had led to Israel receiving funding and protective technology like Iron Dome; Netanyahu argued that he does not accept residency restrictions for Jews and stated that Jerusalem's Arabs and Jews should be able to buy homes wherever they want, saying it was "against the American values" and "anti-peace" to demand ethnic purification as a condition for peace. Jeffrey Goldberg of The Atlantic reported that the relationship between Netanyahu and the White House had reached a new low due to disputes over settlement policies and Netanyahu's contempt for the US administration's Middle East understanding. On 2 December 2014, Netanyahu fired ministers Yair Lapid and Tzipi Livni, leading to government dissolution and new elections on 17 March 2015. In 2015, Netanyahu delivered a speech to the United States Congress, marking his third such address; the day before, Time reported he tried to block a meeting between US lawmakers and Mossad head Tamir Pardo, who was warning against imposing sanctions on Iran. Israeli consuls expected fierce negative reactions from US Jewish communities and allies, with seven American Jewish lawmakers recommending a private meeting on Iran instead. Netanyahu claimed to speak for all Jews worldwide, a claim disputed by others in the Jewish community. As the 2015 election approached, Netanyahu answered "indeed" when asked whether a Palestinian state would not be established in his term, stating that supporting a Palestinian state equated to yielding territory to radical Islamic terrorists; however, he reiterated that he did not want a one-state solution and maintained his support for a peaceful, sustainable two-state solution. In the 2015 election, Netanyahu's Likud won 30 mandates, the highest number of seats in the Knesset; President Rivlin granted him an extension until 6 May 2015 to form a coalition, which he completed within two hours of the deadline. His coalition included Jewish Home, United Torah Judaism, Kulanu, and Shas. In August 2015, the government approved a two-year budget including agricultural reforms, lowering import duties to reduce food prices, deregulating construction approvals to lower housing costs and speed up infrastructure, and financial sector reforms to boost competition and lower fees. The government ultimately compromised by removing some key agricultural reforms. In October 2015, Netanyahu caused controversy by claiming that Haj Amin al-Husseini gave Adolf Hitler the idea of exterminating Jews during the Second World War; this claim is dismissed by most historians, who note al-Husseini's meeting with Hitler occurred about five months after mass murder began, and Israeli academics such as Yehuda Bauer and Moshe Zimmermann criticized the claim as "completely idiotic" and a form of Holocaust denial. In March 2016, Netanyahu's coalition faced a crisis as ultra-Orthodox members threatened to withdraw over proposed non-Orthodox prayer space at the Western Wall, stating they would leave if the government offered official state recognition of Conservative and Reform Judaism. On 23 December 2016, the US, under the Obama administration, abstained from United Nations Security Council Resolution 2334, allowing it to pass; on 28 December, US Secretary of State John Kerry strongly criticized Israel and its settlement policies. Netanyahu strongly criticized both the resolution and Kerry's speech; on 6 January 2017, the Israeli government withdrew its annual dues from UNESCO, totaling $6 million. In February 2017, Netanyahu became the first serving Israeli prime minister to visit Australia, accompanied by his wife Sara, and the visit included business delegations and bilateral agreements; he recalled that Australian Light Horse regiments liberated Beersheba in World War I, beginning a 100-year relationship. In October 2017, shortly after the US announced similar action, Netanyahu's government announced it was leaving UNESCO due to perceived anti-Israel actions, making the decision official in December 2017; the Israeli government formally notified UNESCO of the withdrawal in late December 2017. In April 2018, Netanyahu accused Iran of failing to uphold its obligations under the Iran nuclear deal, presenting over 100,000 documents on Iran's nuclear program; Iran denounced the presentation as "propaganda." Netanyahu praised the 2018 North Korea–United States Singapore Summit, commending President Donald Trump and calling it a step toward eliminating nuclear weapons on the Korean Peninsula. In July 2018, the Knesset passed the Nation-State Bill, a Basic Law supported by Netanyahu's coalition, seen as a sign of advancing a right-wing agenda.
